classification.scheme: UK linear television issues no per-programme age rating. No certificate of any kind is recorded for this asset.

basis.why: Fixes who 'children' are for every operative rule below: people under fifteen.

hours.permitted: any time, including the stated 11:00 slot
hours.with_technical_measure: n/a, no technical measure is needed or relied on

basis.why: The watershed bites on material unsuitable for children. Read against the three observations, none records material of that kind: a minor accidental injury with no blood (o1), ordinary food preparation (o2), and a glass of wine tasted with a meal (o3). The rule is the only bright-line time bound in the slice and it is not engaged, so no hour is barred.

decisions.axis_note: All three axes come back clear and they do so independently. There is no classification to issue, no hour barred, and no condition imposed. The absence of a rating is not what permits the 11:00 slot; the slot is permitted because no rule in the slice restricts the hour for this content.
decisions.reasoning:
Absolute prohibitions first. UK-GEN-001 bars material that might SERIOUSLY impair the development of under-eighteens. The bar is deliberately higher than ordinary harm. A nicked finger treated with a plaster and shown without blood, a knife-skills demonstration, and a glass of wine tasted alongside a dish do not approach it. UK-SEX-001, UK-FLM-001 and UK-FLM-006 require sexual material or a film certificate; neither exists here. No absolute prohibition bites.

Taking the observations in turn. o3 (wine) is the one observation that maps to a rule with a time bound, UK-DRG-001. That rule has two limbs. The first covers programmes made primarily for children; the stated service is free-to-air general entertainment, which is not a children's service, and nothing else in the description supports that reading. The second limb bars alcohol being condoned, encouraged or glamorised before the watershed. Its trigger is treatment, not presence: the observation records wine poured alongside a finished dish and tasted, with no descriptor supporting condoning, encouragement or glamorisation. Neither limb is engaged, so UK-DRG-001 imposes no hour.

o2 (knife skills) maps to UK-IMI-001, which covers dangerous behaviour or behaviour easily imitable by children in a manner that is harmful. Ordinary food preparation in a cookery programme is not that. Were it engaged, the rule is conditional on editorial justification and the demonstration is the programme's own subject matter, so it would be satisfied on the face of it. The rule is not relied on either way.

o1 (minor injury) maps to no rule in the slice. It was extracted under offence_general only because the controlled vocabulary has no value for a minor injury, which RUN 1 flagged. UK-OFF-001 turns on material which may cause offence; a plaster on a cut finger is not that.

That leaves the scheduling rules. UK-SCH-001, UK-SCH-004, UK-SCH-006, UK-SCH-008, UK-SCH-010 and UK-SCH-011 all presuppose material that is unsuitable for children and ask how the hour, the ramp or the calendar should move for it. With nothing unsuitable recorded, none of them has anything to operate on. UK-DEF-002, UK-DEF-003, UK-CTX-010 and UK-CTX-011 are definitions: they shape how an operative rule is read and cannot themselves set an hour or impose a condition, so none appears in basis.

The result is that twenty-one rules were read and none bites. That is the answer, not a reason to escalate.

classification.scheme: French five-category scheme. Category I is the all-audiences category and carries no pictogram.

basis.why: Category I covers programmes for all audiences. Nothing recorded reaches the next category up: FR-CLS-002 requires scenes liable to shock under-tens, and a nicked finger shown without blood, a knife-skills demonstration and a glass of wine tasted with a meal do not.

hours.permitted: any time, including the stated 11:00 slot

basis.why: Every French hour restriction in the slice attaches to a category: FR-SCH-001 to category II, FR-SCH-002 and FR-SCH-004 to category III, FR-SCH-005 to category IV, FR-SCH-007 and FR-CV-003 to category V. The content is category I, so none of them attaches and no hour is barred.

decisions.axis_note: France does issue a classification where the UK does not, and it is category I. Note that the category is what the hours hang off here: in France the classification drives the hour, which is the opposite of the UK answer above, where the hour turns on the content and not on any rating. Same outcome, different route.
decisions.reasoning:
FR-LAW-001 bars programmes liable to SERIOUSLY harm (nuire gravement) the development of minors. As with its UK counterpart the bar is higher than ordinary harm, and nothing recorded approaches it. FR-PRO-001, FR-PRO-002 and FR-PRO-003 require pornographic material or an offence to human dignity; none is recorded.

Classification is the operative question in France, because every hour restriction in the slice hangs off a category. FR-CLS-002 is the first restrictive category and needs certain scenes liable to shock minors under ten. Taking the three observations: a minor accidental injury with no blood shown and described as brief, a knife-skills demonstration in a domestic kitchen, and a glass of wine poured alongside a dish and tasted. None is a scene liable to shock a child under ten. The content is therefore category I, which carries no pictogram and no hour restriction.

With category I settled, FR-SCH-001, FR-SCH-002, FR-SCH-004, FR-SCH-005, FR-SCH-007 and FR-CV-003 all fall away: each attaches to a category this content does not hold. FR-FLM-001 and FR-FLM-002 concern cinema visas carried over to television, and this is a television series episode with no visa.

A gap worth recording rather than hiding: the French slice contains no rule at all for alcohol, for imitable behaviour, or for general offence, while the UK slice contains rules for each. Here that absence changes nothing, because the UK rules were not triggered either. On content where they did bite, France would return silence and it would look like permission.

One correction to an earlier reading of this slice. It is tempting to record the wine, the knife skills and the injury as matching no French rule, because no French row carries those content categories. That would be wrong. The French scheme is category-first: FR-CLS-002 asks whether CERTAIN SCENES are liable to shock minors under ten, and that question is asked of all three observations together. They are evaluated, and they fail to reach the threshold. An unmatched topic category is not an unexamined observation, and reporting it as a gap would send a clean decision to a person on the strength of a difference in drafting style between two regulators.

rules_checked_not_triggered.why_not: Nothing approaching 'nuire gravement'. The most severe observation is a nicked finger shown without blood.

Evaluates ALL THREE observations, not one of them. The French scheme classifies the programme as a whole against 'scenes liable to shock minors under ten' rather than matching topics to separate rules, so the absence of a French alcohol or imitable-behaviour rule is the scheme working as designed, not a hole in the table.
Category III needs a cinema ban for under-twelves or material liable to disturb them. Neither exists.
The category V eligibility gate is reached only for category V content. This is category I.
Total prohibition applies to category V on ineligible services. Not category V.
Attaches to category II. The content is category I.
Attaches to category III.
The category III derogation is reached only for category III content.
Attaches to category IV.
Attaches to category V.
A cinema visa may indicate a television category. This asset has no cinema visa.
The reclassification procedure applies to works with a visa at least twenty years old. No visa exists.

cross_country_note: Both countries permit the 11:00 transmission with no condition, but by different routes. The UK issues no rating and the hour turns directly on whether the content is unsuitable for children, which it is not. France issues a rating, category I, and the hour follows from the category, because every French hour restriction in the slice attaches to a category. The two agree here only because the content is benign. The asymmetry worth flagging is coverage rather than outcome: three of the three observations map to at least one UK rule and none of the three maps to any French rule, so the French clearance rests on the classification scheme alone rather than on topic rules that were read and set aside.
